description: In 2018 the Rhine transport sector went through a low water crisis in which large cargo vessels could no longer navigate some sections of the river, disrupting inland waterway transport. This study by Julie Gobert and Florence Rudolf, published in Frontiers in Climate in January 2023, asks how the crisis pushed port authorities and their customers to consider risks to their assets and operations and to build a shared response. Inspired by the Impact Chain methodology, it applied a step-by-step protocol of focus groups and interviews in which stakeholders affected by low water identified their individual and common vulnerabilities and possible pathways. Of these, the transitional infrastructural pathway, which aims to raise water levels by using Lake Constance as a reservoir or creating new storage areas and to deepen the channel at Kaub and Maxau, was seen as the most suitable because it is a technical, well-controlled short-term solution; the authors read it as an example of infrastructure lock-in. The discussion stresses that new processes and intermodal organisation are needed in the long term. Coverage: Rhine ports and their customers, centred on the Upper Rhine. Access: open-access article. Licence and cost: CC BY, free. Caveats: qualitative stakeholder work without a hydraulic or freight model. It informs climate adaptation and resilience planning for drought-prone waterways and ports. It relates to the BfG Rhine water level forecasts, PEGELONLINE gauges and the CCNR market observation data in the catalogue, which count low water days.
